title: Puzzles & critical reasoning
examples: How can I identify an unstated assumption in a passage?
What is the difference between weakening and attacking an argument?
Can you give me an example of a causal assumption?

explain.say: Today we are looking at making arguments stronger or weaker.

items: Weakening shows the argument is flawed.

explain.say: An assumption is something the argument takes for granted.
We strengthen an argument by adding supporting evidence.
We weaken an argument by pointing out a flaw or exception.
For example, if a study shows ice cream sales rise, it does not mean heat causes ice cream sales.

draw.text: Ice cream sales rise, but not necessarily because of heat.

explain.say: In real life, a company assumes all customers prefer its product.

faq.q: What is the difference between an assumption and a conclusion?
faq.a: The conclusion is what the argument tries to prove using evidence. An assumption is an unstated belief that the argument relies upon to connect the evidence to the conclusion.
asks: How do I spot an assumption?
Is an assumption the same as a premise?

faq.q: When should I use a statement to weaken an argument?
faq.a: You should use it when the statement introduces new information that contradicts the argument's necessary link. Look for exceptions or alternative causes.
asks: Can a single fact weaken a whole argument?

faq.q: Does strengthening an argument mean finding more facts?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Sometimes, strengthening means showing that the assumption is highly probable or necessary for the conclusion to hold.
asks: Is it always better to add more evidence?
What is the best way to strengthen a weak point?

faq.a: No, an assumption can be true in the real world, but the argument fails if the assumption is not logically required to bridge the gap between evidence and conclusion.
asks: If an assumption is true, does the argument still fail?
Must an assumption be proven false to weaken the argument?

faq.q: If I weaken an argument, do I have to provide a better alternative?
faq.a: No, you only need to show that the original argument is flawed or incomplete. You do not need to provide the perfect replacement argument.
asks: Do I need to suggest a better conclusion?
Is pointing out a flaw enough for a good answer?

facts: An assumption is an unstated premise necessary for the conclusion.
Strengthening evidence makes the connection between premises and conclusion stronger.
Weakening evidence introduces a possibility that undermines the conclusion.
Causation must be established; correlation alone is not proof.

quiz.say: Argument: All students who study history pass the test. Therefore, studying history is the best way to pass.

options.show: History is the only subject taught in school.
options.say: History is the only subject taught in school.

options.show: Passing the test requires memorizing dates.
options.say: Passing the test requires memorizing dates.

options.show: There might be other subjects that help pass the test.
options.say: There might be other subjects that help pass the test.

options.show: Students who study history are naturally smart.
options.say: Students who study history are naturally smart.

quiz.why: This correctly weakens the argument by suggesting other possibilities besides history.

wrong.0: This is an overstatement and not directly related to the conclusion's weakness.
wrong.1: This assumes the mechanism of passing, which is not the strongest point of attack.
wrong.3: This is too far from the original claim and introduces unrelated information.

quiz.say: Argument: Since the city invested in new bike lanes, bike usage has increased. Therefore, the bike lanes caused the increase.

options.show: The city must have spent too much money on bike lanes.
options.say: The city must have spent too much money on bike lanes.

options.show: Bike lanes are only good for young people.
options.say: Bike lanes are only good for young people.

options.show: Bike lanes are unsafe for experienced riders.
options.say: Bike lanes are unsafe for experienced riders.

options.show: Perhaps the city also ran a big public awareness campaign.
options.say: Perhaps the city also ran a big public awareness campaign.

quiz.why: This correctly weakens the argument by suggesting an alternative cause besides the bike lanes.

wrong.0: The argument is about causation, not the cost or budget of the lanes.
wrong.1: This changes the scope of the argument rather than challenging the cause-effect link.
wrong.2: This attacks the quality of the lanes, not the assumed cause of the usage increase.

quiz.say: Argument: Because the rainforest canopy is so diverse, it must be the most important ecosystem on Earth.

options.show: The canopy is better for human habitation than the ocean.
options.say: The canopy is better for human habitation than the ocean.

options.show: It ignores the vital role of deep ocean currents in global climate.
options.say: It ignores the vital role of deep ocean currents in global climate.

options.show: The rainforest canopy is always hotter than the ocean.
options.say: The rainforest canopy is always hotter than the ocean.

options.show: Only rainforests have this level of biodiversity.
options.say: Only rainforests have this level of biodiversity.

quiz.why: This correctly weakens the argument by introducing a different, equally important system.

wrong.0: This introduces a subjective value judgment (human habitation) instead of a scientific counterpoint.
wrong.2: This compares two unrelated physical properties instead of challenging the 'most important' claim.
wrong.3: This is an absolute claim that doesn't weaken the argument's core logic.
